lesson.title: Twenty Letters, One Alphabet: Meet the Amino Acids
lesson.summary: Amino acids are small organic molecules built around a central carbon atom that link together to build proteins, and it is the chemistry of their variable side chains that gives proteins their enormous range of shapes and jobs.
lesson.body:
Every amino acid shares the same basic skeleton: a central carbon, called the alpha carbon, bonded to four things. Two of those four are functional groups you should already recognize: an amino group (-NH2) and a carboxyl group (-COOH). The third is a single hydrogen atom. The fourth is a variable side chain, usually written as the R group, and that side chain is the only thing that changes from one amino acid to the next. Cells build proteins from twenty standard amino acids, and every one of them follows this same amino group, carboxyl group, hydrogen, R group pattern around the alpha carbon.

The R group is where the real chemistry happens. Some R groups are small and nonpolar, like the single hydrogen atom that makes glycine the simplest amino acid, or the bulky hydrocarbon rings and chains of leucine, valine, and phenylalanine, which avoid water. Others are polar but uncharged, such as the hydroxyl-bearing side chains of serine and threonine. A few carry a full negative charge at cellular pH, like the carboxylate side chains of aspartate and glutamate, while others, like lysine and arginine, carry a positive charge. This range, from oily and water avoiding to charged and water loving, is exactly why twenty different amino acids can build proteins that behave in twenty different ways.

At the pH found inside cells, amino acids do not sit around neutral. The amino group picks up an extra proton and becomes positively charged (NH3+), while the carboxyl group loses its proton and becomes negatively charged (COO-). A molecule carrying both a positive and a negative charge at once is called a zwitterion, and this dual charge is part of why free amino acids dissolve so readily in the watery environment of the cytoplasm.

The side chain identity of an amino acid is not a minor detail, it can be the difference between health and disease. Sickle cell anemia is caused by a single amino acid substitution in hemoglobin's beta chain: at position six, the normal glutamate, which is negatively charged and water loving, is replaced by valine, which is small and water avoiding. That one change makes deoxygenated hemoglobin molecules stick to each other and polymerize into rigid fibers, distorting red blood cells into a sickle shape. Nothing about the rest of the protein changed, only one side chain out of hundreds, which shows just how much chemical information a single R group carries.

Humans can synthesize eleven of the twenty standard amino acids from other molecules, but the remaining nine, called the essential amino acids, must come from food because our cells lack the enzymes to build them. Once amino acids are available, whether made in the body or eaten in a meal, cells link them together in long chains to build proteins, the molecules that carry out most of the actual work inside a cell. Understanding the twenty amino acids and their side chains is the necessary first step before looking at how they are actually joined together, which is the subject of the peptide bond.
